lead: Both readings speak of love that imitates God. Ephesians tells the baptized to be imitators of God, as beloved children, and to live in love as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us. In John, Jesus gives his commandment, “love one another as I have loved you,” and calls his disciples no longer servants but friends. On the eve of the Ascension the Lord leaves his friends one law to keep until he comes again: the law of his own love.

r.h: Imitators of God, as beloved children
set: Ephesians is written in the name of Paul. Many scholars think a disciple of Paul composed it; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. The Church reads it as part of the apostolic witness. Chapters 4–6 draw out the way of life that follows from being one body in Christ. Just before this reading the letter says, “be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you” (4:32). Today’s verses continue: forgiven children should resemble their Father.
str: vv. 1–2: imitate God; live in love as Christ loved us, a fragrant offering.
vv. 3–4: what has no place among saints: impurity, greed, vulgar talk; instead, thanksgiving.
v. 5: no inheritance in the kingdom for the impure and the greedy, who are idolaters.
kw: From the word that gives us “mimic”. Children copy their parents. Here believers are called imitators of God himself; elsewhere in the New Testament they are told to imitate Christ and the apostles.
The language of Old Testament sacrifice, whose smoke was a “pleasing odour” to the Lord (Exodus 29:18). Christ’s self-giving on the Cross is the true sacrifice, pleasing to the Father.
vv: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children,
The command is possible only because we are already beloved. We do not earn God’s love by imitating him; we imitate him because we are loved.
and live in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God.
“Live” is literally “walk”: love is a daily road. Its measure is the Cross.
but instead, let there be thanksgiving.
The remedy for an unclean tongue is not silence but thanksgiving. The Greek word is eucharistia.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the moral life of Christians is rooted in their dignity as children of God, called to imitate the Father’s holiness (CCC 1694, quoting this verse). The sacrifice of Christ, the “fragrant offering”, is made present in every Holy Qurbana, and the Church offers herself with it (CCC 1368).

set: These words belong to the Last Supper discourse, just after the image of the vine and the branches (15:1–10). Jesus has told the disciples to abide in him as branches abide in the vine. Now he explains what abiding means: keeping his commandment, which is love. The passage begins and ends with the command “love one another” (vv. 12, 17).
str: v. 11: my joy in you, your joy complete.
vv. 12–13: my commandment: love one another as I have loved you; no greater love than to lay down one’s life.
vv. 14–15: you are my friends; no longer servants.
vv. 16–17: I chose you to bear fruit that lasts; love one another.
kw: In the Old Testament Abraham is called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8), and the Lord spoke to Moses “as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jesus gives this title to all his disciples.
The initiative is the Lord’s. Disciples in Jesus’ time usually chose their rabbi; here the Master chooses his disciples.
vv: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
The measure is new: not “as yourself” but “as I have loved you”.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
Spoken a few hours before the Cross. Jesus does not only teach this love; he is about to show it.
but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
Friendship is shown by sharing secrets. The disciples are friends because Jesus has opened to them the heart of the Father.
The fruit is love, and love that comes from Christ does not pass away (1 Corinthians 13:8).
ch: The Catechism cites this commandment when it teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, loving his own “to the end” and so making manifest the Father’s love (CCC 1823). It also teaches that chastity blossoms in friendship, and cites “I have called you friends” (CCC 2347).

study: Ephesians calls me to imitate God “as beloved children”. Do I live as someone already loved, or as someone trying to earn love?
Jesus calls his disciples friends. What would change in my prayer if I spoke to him as a friend?
